analysis.one_liner: Requires hotels and short-term rentals to show all mandatory fees in the advertised price.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 384-25 on June 11, 2024, but it never received a vote in the Senate and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone selling hotel rooms, motels, inns, or short-term rentals to include every mandatory fee when advertising or displaying a reservation price, instead of adding 'resort fees' and similar charges at checkout. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rule. It would also set a single national standard that could override some state laws on lodging price advertising, and it does not cover bookings made through corporate or government travel programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday travelers booking hotels and short-term rentals. Today, a room can be advertised at a low base price while mandatory 'resort' or 'destination' fees are only revealed late in the booking process, making it hard to comparison-shop. The bill would force the full price into the ad, so shoppers could see the true cost up front. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would have the power to sue violators, under the same penalties as other deceptive advertising cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Travelers booking hotels and vacation rentals

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits advertising, displaying, or offering a reservation price that does not include each mandatory fee, for hotels, motels, inns, and short-term rentals.
The Federal Trade Commission can enforce violations the same way it enforces other unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents.
The requirement applies to direct bookings, third-party sites, and metasearch referral services, so the disclosure follows the price wherever it is shown.

analysis.who_pays: Hotel chains, motels, and short-term rental operators lose the ability to attract customers with a low headline price and add mandatory fees later, which likely erodes the extra revenue those fees generate. Online booking platforms and metasearch sites must show all-in prices too. Anyone selling through corporate, government, or institutional travel programs is exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hotels, short-term rentals, and booking platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws that 'affect the manner' in which lodging prices are advertised, which could override stricter state fee-disclosure rules; states keep only their contract, tort, fraud, and data-breach laws.
The disclosure requirement does not apply to bookings made through corporate, government, or institutional travel management programs.
The ban covers only mandatory fees assessed by the provider and paid directly by the consumer; certain taxes and government-imposed fees are excluded from the definition.
It applies only to reservations made after the law takes effect, one year after enactment, so past bookings are untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For travelers, the core benefit is straightforward: the price in the ad becomes the price you pay for provider fees, ending surprise resort and destination fees at checkout. The main cost is borne by lodging companies, whose drip-pricing practice is designed to make rooms look cheaper than they are. The genuine design flaw is the preemption section: states that already passed tougher disclosure laws could see those rules displaced by the federal standard, so in some states the bill might trade stronger local rules for a weaker national one.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it overwhelmingly by voice of a near-unanimous vote, but it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the next day and never received a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 1, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The committee took it up almost immediately, ordering it reported by a vote of 43-0 in December 2023, and formally reported it in May 2024.

On June 11, 2024, the House passed the bill under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure (which requires a two-thirds majority) by a vote of 384-25; all 204 voting Democrats supported it, and 180 Republicans supported it while 25 opposed.

The Senate received the bill on June 12, 2024 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because the Congress ended, the bill died; it would have to be reintroduced to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hotel chains, short-term rental operators, and booking platforms keep advertising low base prices and adding mandatory fees at checkout, since the Senate never acted on the ban.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hotel and booking companies that charge add-on fees

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held markups in December 2023 and ordered the bill reported unanimously, 43-0; formally reported it in May 2024 with a written report.

for.name: Rep. Gus Bilirakis
for.role: House member who managed floor passage
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill on the House floor on June 11, 2024.

for.name: 384 House members
for.what_they_did: Voted to pass the bill, including all 204 voting Democrats and 180 Republicans.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee where the bill was parked
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 12, 2024, referred it to itself, and took no further action; the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: 25 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage, the only 'no' votes on the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was nearly unanimous but not perfectly so: every voting Democrat (204) supported the bill, while 180 of 205 voting Republicans did, with 25 Republicans opposed. The real opposition was Senate inaction rather than a party-line fight.

industries.industry: Hotels, motels, and short-term rental operators
industries.note: The bill takes away the ability to advertise a low base price and add mandatory fees like resort fees at checkout, which is the profit mechanic the bill targets. At the same time, its national preemption section could displace stricter state disclosure laws and gives the industry one uniform federal standard instead of a patchwork.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and metasearch platforms
industries.note: Platforms and referral sites that display reservation prices must show all-in prices, reducing flexibility to sort listings by base rate. Preemption also spares them from navigating conflicting state advertising rules.
